text: Every IF example last lesson controlled exactly one statement. That's not a coincidence — it's a hard rule in T-SQL, and it catches almost everyone at least once.

Look at this carefully. It looks like both the PRINT and the SELECT belong inside the IF, because they're indented the same way. They don't. IF only controls the single statement immediately after it — the PRINT. That SELECT runs every single time, no matter what the condition says. T-SQL does not care about indentation at all. This is a genuinely common beginner trap.

BEGIN and END fix this by actually grouping statements into one block. Now both PRINT statements inside the first BEGIN-END only run if product count is over 500 — they're genuinely bundled together as one unit, and IF treats that whole block as a single thing to run or skip.

And here's a habit worth adopting: this course wraps IF branches in BEGIN-END even when there's only one statement inside. It's purely defensive — if someone comes back later and adds a second statement to that branch, which happens constantly in real code, the block already exists and behaves correctly, instead of silently breaking the way our very first example did.

One statement without BEGIN-END, any number of statements with it — and this course always uses it, just in case. Next lesson: WHILE loops, for repeating code until a condition changes. See you there.
